issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise organized around war-zone trauma appraisals of injustice/accountability and a threat pattern of hypervigilance, startle, and concentration problems. Self-harm to release overwhelming feelings introduces a distinct affect-regulation strategy that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and sits poorly with the formulation, where Maladaptive Strategies has only a modest reciprocal link with Threat and no links from Negative Appraisals. Given the rest of the profile, a more threat-management strategy would be expected; this item feels clinically out of pattern rather than impossible.

vignette:
Kwame is a 33-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a social media manager for a mid-sized nonprofit in Atlanta. He is married, and until recently his colleagues and his wife alike described him as steady, warm, and unflappable. He presented to the clinic following a referral from his primary care physician, with a PCL-5 score of 68 and a quiet insistence that he was "not handling things the way I should."

Three years ago, Kwame volunteered for an eight-month deployment with a humanitarian relief organization operating in a conflict zone in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. He had done similar work before and believed he was prepared. What he was not prepared for was the ambush on a convoy he was travelling with during his sixth month - a coordinated attack that killed two local drivers and left two aid workers critically wounded. Kwame was uninjured in any way that could be photographed. He spent four hours pinned behind a vehicle, listening to the sounds of sustained gunfire and the voices of men he could not help, before government forces arrived. He was evacuated within days and told, in the bureaucratic language of incident reports, that the matter was under investigation. It was not, to his knowledge, ever resolved. No one was held to account. The organization issued a statement. Kwame flew home to Atlanta.

In the months that followed, Kwame came to carry a belief that felt less like a thought and more like a physical fact: that the world had looked at what happened to him and to the men who died and had simply turned away. He was certain that what had occurred was a profound injustice, and the absence of any consequence for those responsible confirmed, in his mind, that such violence was not aberrant but tolerated - which meant it could happen again, anywhere, to anyone. He had come to believe, most painfully, that he could not rely on himself; the memory of those four hours, in which he had done nothing, had calcified into evidence of some fundamental inadequacy. These appraisals did not remain abstract. They fed directly into a state of chronic threat readiness that now organized much of his waking life. He was superalert in a way that exhausted him - scanning parking lots, tracking exits in restaurants, startling violently at the sound of a car backfiring or a door slamming in the office corridor. He found it nearly impossible to concentrate on sustained work, losing the thread of a sentence mid-draft, forgetting what he had opened a browser tab to find.

The hypervigilance and the startle responses were distressing enough that Kwame began, almost without deciding to, to manage them through avoidance. He stopped letting himself think about the convoy. When images surfaced - the angle of light on the road, the particular quality of the silence before the shooting began - he learned to slide away from them, to detach himself so efficiently that the memories felt like footage from someone else's life. He also began constantly scanning his environment, a habit that had started as vigilance but had become its own compulsive ritual, as though checking the room could forestall what checking the room could never actually prevent. The irony was not lost on him, though he lacked the language to name it: the strategies he used to manage the feeling of threat kept him perpetually oriented toward threat. Sitting at his desk managing content calendars and engagement metrics, he would find himself pausing every few minutes to look toward the office door - a behavior his colleagues had begun to notice and that had made him feel, in his own words, "like a man pretending to be fine at a job that requires him to be fine."

His wife had gently and then less gently raised her concern. It was her observation - that he seemed to be disappearing from their evenings together, present in body but somewhere far away - that finally moved him to make the appointment. What Kwame said he feared most was that this was simply who he was now. What he hoped, though he offered this quietly, was that someone might be able to tell him otherwise.
